title: How One Mom Built a Dyslexia School After Schools Failed Her Daughter
guestBio: Cathy Johnson is a licensed Speech-Language Pathologist and the founder of The Johnson Academy — the only school for children with dyslexia in South Orange County — and the Speech, Language and Learning Center in San Juan Capistrano. After her own daughter was diagnosed with dyslexia in kindergarten, Cathy refused to wait and watch, eventually building a school, consulting for school districts, and co-creating an Orton-Gillingham teacher-training program at the University of La Verne. Her nonprofit, Ready to Read, funds scholarships so that no family is turned away for financial reasons.
excerpt: Speech-language pathologist Cathy Johnson built a school for kids with dyslexia after the system failed her own daughter — and she has spent 20 years proving there is no such thing as too late. In this episode, she and host Aimee Rickabus break down the third-grade window, what multisensory instruction actually looks like, and why "they'll catch up" is not a plan.
metaDescription: SLP Cathy Johnson built a dyslexia school after schools failed her daughter. Learn the signs, the science, and what every mom needs to know about early intervention.
keyTakeaways: A speech delay at age five is a meaningful warning sign for dyslexia and a reason to screen immediately — not a reason to wait and watch.
The third-grade window is real: early intervention before third grade produces dramatically better outcomes than remediation attempted later in a child's education.
Dyslexia is a learning difference, not a disability or a reflection of a child's intelligence, and reframing it that way changes everything for the child and the family.
Accommodations like extra time on tests are support tools, not interventions — they do not teach the brain to read and should never replace structured literacy instruction.
More reading practice using the wrong method does not build skill; it can actually reinforce incorrect patterns, so the method matters as much as the hours put in.
When evaluating a reading specialist or tutor, look for year-long, supervised training in programs like Orton-Gillingham or Wilson — not a weekend certification course.
The problem standing in front of you — a child who cannot read, a school that will not act — can be the very thing that reveals your purpose, just as it was for Cathy.

quiz.title: What Kind of Advocate Are You When Your Child Needs More?
quiz.description: Every mother who has ever sat across from a teacher and felt something was being missed has a different instinct about what to do next. This quiz helps you understand your natural advocacy style — and how to make it work harder for your child.

A.name: The Fierce Researcher
A.description: When something feels wrong, you go straight to the source — studies, specialists, and second opinions. You trust data over reassurance, and you will not stop until you have a complete picture. Your strength is that you walk into every meeting armed. Your edge to sharpen is learning when to act on what you already know, rather than searching for one more confirmation. This episode will give you the science to back what your gut has already been telling you.

B.name: The Steady Advocate
B.description: You are the calm in the room — the mom who keeps her composure in the IEP meeting, who documents everything, who builds relationships with teachers rather than burning them. You are effective precisely because you are not threatening. Your edge to sharpen is trusting your urgency when calm is no longer serving your child. This episode will show you what it looks like when a mother's steadiness becomes the foundation of a school.

C.name: The Intuitive Protector
C.description: You knew before anyone put a name to it. You watched your child's face when they tried to read, you felt something in the classroom that the report cards were not capturing, and you have been carrying that knowing quietly for longer than you should have had to. Your edge to sharpen is translating your instinct into action that the system will hear. This episode is the language you have been looking for.

D.name: The Purpose-Driven Builder
D.description: You do not just want to solve this for your child — you want to solve it for every child who comes after. You see the gap, and some part of you is already imagining a different way. You might be a teacher, a therapist, a founder-in-waiting, or simply a mother who cannot stop thinking about the other families sitting in the same waiting room. This episode is a roadmap from one woman who felt exactly what you feel — and built something extraordinary because of it.

content:
There is a moment that a lot of mothers know. You are sitting at a parent-teacher conference, watching a teacher nod slowly, and the words coming back to you are let's give it some time or every child develops differently or the one that stings the most: they'll catch up. And somewhere underneath your polite smile, something in you does not believe it — because you live with this child, you watch this child, and you know something is being missed.

This episode is for you.

Host Aimee Rickabus opens by sharing something personal: her oldest son was diagnosed with dyslexia in first grade. After his very first day at The Johnson Academy, he came home and said, "Mom, no one ever taught me how to read before." He was not being dramatic. He was telling the exact truth — and that sentence is the whole reason this conversation exists.

When the System Says Wait, and a Mother Says No

Cathy Johnson did not set out to build a school. She set out to help her daughter. When that daughter was diagnosed with dyslexia in kindergarten, Cathy — already a licensed Speech-Language Pathologist — did everything right. She got the diagnosis. She sought intervention. She watched and advocated and pushed. And then, in fifth grade, her daughter woke up one morning and said, "I'm not going to school anymore."

That was the moment. Not a business plan, not a grand vision — a mother standing in her kitchen at a crossroads, choosing action over acceptance. Twenty years later, The Johnson Academy is the only school for children with dyslexia in all of South Orange County. What began as an act of love for one child now serves hundreds of families who found themselves in that same kitchen, hearing that same silence after the school said wait.

Cathy is careful to be precise about what dyslexia is and is not. It is a learning difference, not a reflection of a child's intelligence, character, or effort. Dyslexic children are not lazy. They are not behind because they did not try. They are behind because the reading instruction they received was not designed for the way their brains process language — and that is a curriculum problem, not a child problem.

The Third-Grade Window (and Why It Is Not a Deadline)

One of the most urgent things Cathy shares is the research on early intervention. Before third grade, the brain is still in a window of neuroplasticity that makes rewiring reading pathways significantly more efficient. The earlier a child receives structured, evidence-based literacy instruction, the less remediation they will need later — and the less damage accumulates to their sense of themselves as a learner.

But Cathy is equally urgent about something else: there is no such thing as too late. She has taught a 70-year-old woman to read. That woman wept when she read her first complete sentence. The third-grade window is not a deadline — it is an argument for urgency, not a reason to give up on an older child or adult who has been failed by the system for decades.

For parents of young children, though, the message is clear: a speech delay at age five is not something to monitor quietly. It is a reason to screen. Cathy explains that the same phonological processing challenges that produce a speech problem at five are the same challenges that produce a reading problem at seven — and intervening on the front end of that timeline changes everything.

What Multisensory Instruction Actually Looks Like

You have probably heard the term multisensory learning and maybe pictured something loosely crafty and vaguely educational. Cathy makes it concrete. Structured literacy approaches like Orton-Gillingham and Wilson are built on a simple truth: when you engage more senses at the same time — hearing a sound, seeing the letter, writing it in the air, feeling the movement in your arm — the brain has more pathways to file and retrieve that information. The sound sticks in a way it cannot when it comes only through sight or only through sound.

This also explains why more practice does not work — and can actually make things worse. If a child is practicing an incorrect pattern, repetition reinforces that incorrect pattern. Timed reading tests that panic a child whose processing is already under stress do not build speed; they build anxiety. The method has to change before the hours invested mean anything.

When you are evaluating a specialist, tutor, or program for your child, Cathy says to ask one question: What is your training? A weekend certificate is not enough. You are looking for year-long, supervised, structured training in an evidence-based program. It is not an unreasonable bar — it is the standard that the research demands.

From Purpose to Institution: The Entrepreneurial Layer

What makes this conversation land differently than a typical conversation about dyslexia is that Cathy is also — quietly, practically, genuinely — a founder. She took the risk of building something from nothing, financed it, consulted for school districts to keep the lights on, built a teacher-training pipeline at the University of La Verne, and launched a nonprofit called Ready to Read so that tuition cost would never be the reason a child did not get help.

She talks about what it felt like to make that leap — the fear, the financing, the moment she realized the problem in front of her was not an obstacle but an assignment. The problem standing in front of you might be pointing directly at your purpose. That is not a platitude when it comes from a woman who turned her daughter's crisis into a school that has now served children for two decades.

What Aimee Wants You to Take With You

If your child is struggling to read and the school is telling you to wait, you are not overreacting. Your instinct is data. Early screening — available as young as age four, before a child has even seen a letter — can give you answers the school may not be motivated to find on your timeline. You do not have to wait for a referral. You do not have to wait for third grade. You do not have to wait at all.

And if your child is older, if the window people keep referencing has already passed, Cathy's answer is the same one she opens with: there really isn't a too late. The brain is more adaptable than the system has given you reason to believe. What it needs is the right instruction — not more of the wrong kind, not more patience with a method that was never built for it, but a teacher who knows how to reach it.

That teacher exists. That school exists. And this conversation is a very good place to start.
